summary.text: A binomial-sum identity gives \(2nS(n)=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1=L_{2n}-1\), so integrality would force \(2n\mid L_{2n}-1\); finite residue checks using Fibonacci periods modulo \(4,3,5\) rule this out whenever \(n\) has one of those prime factors. Otherwise, for the least prime factor \(p>5\), roots \(a,b\) of \(x^2-x-1\) over a splitting field turn \(p\mid L_{2n}-1\) into \(a^{12n}=1\), while Frobenius gives \(a^{p^2-1}=1\); since \(n\) is coprime to \(p^2-1\), the order of \(a\) divides \(12\), contradicting the Bézout identity showing that \(x^2-x-1\) and \(x^{12}-1\) can share a root only in characteristics dividing \(320\), hence not for \(p>5\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac1i\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1},
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the denominator of \(S_n\) when it is written in lowest terms. We prove that \(S_n\) is not an integer whenever \(n>1\), which is equivalent to \(a(n)\ne 1\).

Write \(F_r\) for the Fibonacci numbers, with \(F_0=0\), \(F_1=1\), and \(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\). We first turn the defining binomial sum into a Fibonacci expression.

For \(1\le i\le n\), the elementary binomial identity
\[
2n\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}
 =i\left(\binom{2n-i}{i}+\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}\right)
\]
holds. Indeed, if \(C=\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}\), then
\[
(2n-i)C=i\binom{2n-i}{i},
\]
and adding \(iC\) to both sides gives the displayed identity. Dividing by \(i\) and summing gives
\[
2nS_n=
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i}{i}
+
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}.
\tag{1}
\]

We use the standard diagonal binomial formula
\[
F_{m+1}=\sum_{j\ge 0}\binom{m-j}{j}.
\tag{2}
\]
Only the terms with \(j\le m-j\) are nonzero, so the sum is finite. Formula (2) follows, for example, by observing that both sides satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence, with the same initial values.

Taking \(m=2n\) in (2), the nonzero indices are \(0\le j\le n\). The \(j=0\) term is \(1\), and hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i}{i}=F_{2n+1}-1.
\]
For the second sum in (1), put \(j=i-1\). Then \(0\le j\le n-1\), and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-2-j}{j}
 =F_{2n-1}.
\]
Consequently, for every positive \(n\),
\[
2nS_n=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1.
\tag{3}
\]
Set
\[
L_n:=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1.
\]
Thus \(S_n=L_n/(2n)\). In particular, if the reduced denominator of \(S_n\) were \(1\), then \(S_n\) would be an integer, and therefore
\[
2n\mid L_n.
\tag{4}
\]
We will prove that (4) is impossible for every \(n>1\).

We first establish the obstruction used when the least prime factor of \(n\) is greater than \(5\).

**Large-prime obstruction.** Let \(p>5\) be prime and let \(n>0\). If
\[
\gcd(n,p^2-1)=1,
\tag{5}
\]
then
\[
p\nmid L_n.
\tag{6}
\]

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(p\mid L_n\). Work over the field \(\mathbb F_p\), and let \(K\) be a finite splitting field of
\[
f(X)=X^2-X-1.
\]
Choose a root \(\alpha\in K\), and put \(\beta=1-\alpha\). Both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are roots of \(f\), and
\[
\alpha+\beta=1,
\qquad
\alpha\beta=-1.
\tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(\alpha\ne0\).

For every positive integer \(r\),
\[
\alpha^r+\beta^r
 =F_{r+1}+(F_{r+1}-F_r).
\tag{8}
\]
Here the right side is interpreted in \(K\). To prove (8), note that each root \(u\) satisfies \(u^2=u+1\), and hence
\[
u^{r+2}=u^{r+1}+u^r.
\]
Thus the left side satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence in \(r\). The formula is immediate for \(r=1\), since \(\alpha+\beta=1\), and for \(r=2\), since \(\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+1)+(\beta+1)=3\). These are also the corresponding values on the right, and induction proves (8).

Apply (8) with \(r=2n\). Since
\[
F_{2n+1}-F_{2n}=F_{2n-1},
\]
we obtain
\[
\alpha^{2n}+\beta^{2n}=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}.
\]
The assumption \(p\mid L_n\) therefore implies
\[
\alpha^{2n}+\beta^{2n}=1
\tag{9}
\]
in \(K\). By (7),
\[
\alpha^{2n}\beta^{2n}=(\alpha\beta)^{2n}=1.
\]
Put \(x=\alpha^{2n}\). Then \(\beta^{2n}=x^{-1}\), so (9) says
\[
x+x^{-1}=1.
\]
Multiplication by \(x\) gives
\[
x^2-x+1=0.
\]
It follows that \(x^3=-1\), and hence \(x^6=1\). Thus
\[
\alpha^{12n}=1.
\tag{10}
\]

We also have
\[
\alpha^{p^2}=\alpha.
\tag{11}
\]
For completeness, the Frobenius map sends a root of \(f\) to another root: because the characteristic is \(p\),
\[
(\alpha^p)^2-\alpha^p-1=(\alpha^2-\alpha-1)^p=0.
\]
The two roots are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), so either \(\alpha^p=\alpha\) or \(\alpha^p=\beta\). In the first case, applying the \(p\)-th power once more gives \(\alpha^{p^2}=\alpha\). In the second case, since \(p\) is odd,
\[
\beta^p=(1-\alpha)^p=1-\alpha^p=1-\beta=\alpha,
\]
which gives the same conclusion. Since \(\alpha\ne0\), (11) yields
\[
\alpha^{p^2-1}=1.
\tag{12}
\]

Let \(d\) be the multiplicative order of \(\alpha\) in \(K^\times\). Equations (10) and (12) show that
\[
d\mid 12n,
\qquad
d\mid p^2-1.
\]
By (5), every divisor of \(p^2-1\), and in particular \(d\), is coprime to \(n\). Therefore \(d\mid12\), so
\[
\alpha^{12}=1.
\tag{13}
\]

It remains to observe that a root of \(X^2-X-1\) cannot satisfy (13) in characteristic greater than \(5\). The following explicit polynomial identity, valid over every commutative ring, proves this:
\[
A(X)(X^2-X-1)+(144X-232)(X^{12}-1)=320,
\tag{14}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(X)={}&-144X^{11}+88X^{10}-56X^9+32X^8-24X^7+8X^6\\
&-16X^5-8X^4-24X^3-32X^2-56X-88.
\end{aligned}
\]
Identity (14) follows by direct expansion. Evaluating it at \(X=\alpha\), using both \(f(\alpha)=0\) and (13), gives \(320=0\) in \(K\). Thus the characteristic \(p\) divides \(320=2^6\cdot5\). Since \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p=2\) or \(p=5\), contradicting \(p>5\). This proves the large-prime obstruction.

Next we record three elementary small-prime obstructions. We use the following standard periodicity observation. If, modulo an integer \(M\),
\[
F_T\equiv0,
\qquad F_{T+1}\equiv1,
\]
then
\[
F_{r+T}\equiv F_r\pmod M
\tag{15}
\]
for every \(r\). Indeed, the pair \((F_T,F_{T+1})\) equals the initial pair \((F_0,F_1)\) modulo \(M\), and the Fibonacci recurrence determines all subsequent pairs. Equivalently, one may use the Fibonacci addition formula. Repeating (15) shows that \(F_r\pmod M\) depends only on \(r\pmod T\).

1. Modulo \(4\), the Fibonacci residues for indices \(0,1,\ldots,5\) are
\[
0,1,1,2,3,1,
\]
and the next pair is \(0,1\), so the period \(6\) may be used. Suppose \(n\) is positive and even, say \(n=2k\). Then
\[
L_n\equiv F_{4k+1}+F_{4k-1}-1\pmod4.
\]
For \(k\pmod6=0,1,2,3,4,5\), the pair of indices \((4k+1,4k-1)\pmod6\) is respectively
\[
(1,5),(5,3),(3,1),(1,5),(5,3),(3,1).
\]
Using the displayed residue list, the corresponding values of \(L_n\pmod4\) are
\[
1,2,2,1,2,2.
\]
None is zero. Hence
\[
2\mid n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4\nmid L_n.
\tag{16}
\]

2. Modulo \(3\), the Fibonacci residues for indices \(0,1,\ldots,7\) are
\[
0,1,1,2,0,2,2,1,
\]
and the next pair is again \(0,1\), giving period \(8\). Suppose \(n\) is odd and divisible by \(3\), say \(n=3k\). Since both \(n\) and \(3\) are odd, \(k\) is odd. For \(k\pmod8=1,3,5,7\), the index pair
\[
(6k+1,6k-1)\pmod8
\]
is, respectively,
\[
(7,5),(3,1),(7,5),(3,1).
\]
In every case the residue list gives
\[
L_n=F_{6k+1}+F_{6k-1}-1\equiv2\pmod3.
\]
Thus
\[
n\text{ odd and }3\mid n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 3\nmid L_n.
\tag{17}
\]

3. Modulo \(5\), the Fibonacci residues for indices \(0,1,\ldots,19\) are
\[
0,1,1,2,3,0,3,3,1,4,0,4,4,3,2,0,2,2,4,1,
\]
and the next pair is \(0,1\), giving period \(20\). Suppose \(5\mid n\) and \(n\) is odd; write \(n=5k\). Then \(k\) is odd. For every odd residue class of \(k\) modulo \(20\),
\[
10k+1\equiv11\pmod{20},
\qquad
10k-1\equiv9\pmod{20}.
\]
Since \(F_{11}\equiv4\) and \(F_9\equiv4\pmod5\),
\[
L_n\equiv4+4-1\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
Therefore
\[
n\text{ odd and }5\mid n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 5\nmid L_n.
\tag{18}
\]

We now finish the proof. Assume \(n>1\), and suppose for contradiction that \(S_n\) is an integer. By (3), this implies \(2n\mid L_n\).

If \(2\mid n\), then \(4\mid2n\), so \(4\mid L_n\), contradicting (16).

Hence \(n\) is odd. If \(3\mid n\), then \(3\mid2n\), so \(3\mid L_n\), contradicting (17).

We may therefore assume that neither \(2\) nor \(3\) divides \(n\). If \(5\mid n\), then \(5\mid2n\), so \(5\mid L_n\), contradicting (18).

It remains to consider the case in which none of \(2,3,5\) divides \(n\). Let \(p\) be the least prime factor of \(n\). Then \(p>5\). We claim that
\[
\gcd(n,p^2-1)=1.
\tag{19}
\]
Suppose instead that a prime \(q\) divided both \(n\) and \(p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)\). Because \(p\) is the least prime factor of \(n\), we have \(q\ge p\). Since \(q\) is prime and divides \((p-1)(p+1)\), it divides either \(p-1\) or \(p+1\). The first alternative gives \(q\le p-1\), impossible. In the second, \(q\le p+1\). Together with \(q\ge p\), this leaves only \(q=p\) or \(q=p+1\). But \(p\nmid p^2-1\), and \(p+1\) is an even integer greater than \(2\), so it cannot equal the prime \(q\). This proves (19).

Since \(p\mid n\), the assumed divisibility \(2n\mid L_n\) implies \(p\mid L_n\). But (19) allows us to apply the large-prime obstruction, which says that \(p\nmid L_n\). This final contradiction shows that \(S_n\) cannot be an integer.

Therefore, for every integer \(n>1\), the denominator of
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1i\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}
\]
in lowest terms is greater than \(1\). Equivalently, \(a(n)\ne1\) for every \(n>1\).
